title: Emergency Response and DP Event Reporting
description: The TDPO learns the emergency responses that sit outside single-system failures: transferring command to the backup DP station, executing a time-critical escape move under collision threat, and investigating, classifying and reporting a DP station keeping event to the IMCA scheme standard. Professional standard means decisions made without hesitation, procedures followed under time pressure, and events documented well enough that a stranger could reconstruct them from the report alone.
source_reference: IMCA M117 Rev 3.3 — Appendix G (DP System Emergency Drills and Exercises, scenarios G3.5) and Appendix H (DP Station Keeping Event Reporting)

tasks.title: Backup DP Station Changeover
tasks.setup: Vessel settled in DP at datum with the model built. Confirm the backup DP station is powered, available, and showing valid data. Locate your vessel's control transfer procedure and read it once before starting. Note which station currently holds command and record your settled position and heading.
tasks.execute: Hold position for 5 minutes and record your maximum excursion as a baseline. Then treat the primary station as unavailable: transfer command to the backup DP station following the vessel procedure step by step. Continue holding position from the backup station for 10 minutes. Record the time from decision to completed transfer, the position and heading excursion during the transfer, and every alarm generated.
professional_standard: Transfer completed as a continuous deliberate sequence — no backtracking through the procedure
Command confirmed at the backup station and stated out loud (or logged) before releasing attention from the primary
Position excursion during transfer no greater than the baseline excursion recorded in the first 5 minutes
Heading held within 2 degrees throughout
All alarms generated by the transfer acknowledged and understood, not just silenced

fields.label: Time from decision to completed transfer (seconds)

debrief_questions: What checks would you make at the backup station before accepting command, and what could go wrong if you skipped them?
Which failure modes could take out the primary station while leaving the backup healthy? Which failures would take out both?
What happens to the vessel's station keeping in the seconds between the primary station being lost and command being established at the backup?
How would working at 50m from a structure change your decision about whether to transfer command or take the vessel on joystick first?
Why does DP class notation require an independent backup control station at all — what redundancy principle is it protecting?

variants.title: Unplanned Changeover

changes.trigger: Supervising DPO calls the transfer at an unannounced moment during a 15-minute hold

variants.note_to_tdpo: Same procedure, but you no longer choose the moment. Notice how much of your first attempt's smoothness came from being mentally ready.

variants.title: Changeover in Weather
variants.note_to_tdpo: Bigger excursions, less time to think. The procedure does not change — your margin does.

variants.title: Transfer and Return
variants.note_to_tdpo: After 10 minutes at the backup station, transfer command back to the primary. Two transfers, both to standard, in one session.

tasks.title: Collision Threat Escape Move
tasks.vessel_mode_execute: DP position move or JSMH — your choice, justified in debrief
tasks.setup: Vessel settled in DP at datum. Before anything else, plan your escape: assess the environment and decide, out loud or on paper, the direction you would move the vessel if a drifting vessel or object threatened your position, and whether you would use a DP position move or take the vessel on joystick. Then set a random trigger — either the supervising DPO calls it, or use a timer set between 3 and 10 minutes that you cannot see.
tasks.execute: Hold position normally. On the trigger, move the vessel 100m in your pre-planned escape direction as quickly as you can do it safely and in control. Record the time from trigger to first commanded input, time to reach 50m and 100m from datum, maximum speed achieved, and maximum heading deviation. Settle the vessel at the new position with residual velocity below 0.1kts.
professional_standard: First commanded input within 15 seconds of the trigger
Escape direction matches the plan made in setup — no improvising a new direction under pressure
Heading either held throughout or altered deliberately as part of the plan, not lost
Speed built decisively but deceleration planned — vessel settled at 100m without a large overshoot
Residual velocity below 0.1kts at the settled position

fields.label: Time from trigger to first commanded input (seconds)
Control method used (DP move / joystick) and why

debrief_questions: Why did you choose the escape direction you planned — which environmental force were you working with, and which were you accepting working against?
DP position move versus joystick takeover for an escape: what does each give you, what does each cost you, and what would tip your choice one way or the other?
At the maximum speed you reached, roughly what stopping distance did you need — and how does that number change what '100m clear' actually buys you?
How is this manoeuvre different from a planned departure from a worksite, in both technique and mindset?
If the threat direction had been the same as your planned escape direction, what would your alternative have been?

variants.title: Escape With Heading Change
variants.note_to_tdpo: Escape and rotate 45 degrees during the move — as you might to present the stern or reduce beam exposure. Two control problems at once.

variants.title: Escape From Degraded Start

changes.start_condition: One thruster deselected before the hold begins

variants.note_to_tdpo: Reduced authority changes your acceleration, your stopping distance, and possibly your best direction. Re-plan the escape in setup accordingly.

tasks.title: DP Event Investigation, Classification and Report
tasks.setup: Arrange with the supervising DPO for one degradation to be injected at some point during a 15-minute hold — a reference deselection, a sensor deviation, a thruster deselection — without telling you the time or the nature. If working alone, use the simulator's scenario or failure injection function on a delay. Have the three IMCA station keeping event category definitions written in front of you: DP incident (total loss of DP capability), DP undesired event (loss of redundancy and/or compromised capability), DP observation (neither, but worth sharing). Start a written timeline with the session start time as entry one.
tasks.execute: Hold position. When the event occurs, respond to it correctly and log your actions with times as you go. Once the vessel is stable, reconstruct the full event timeline from the DP alarm and event log, compare it against your own handwritten timeline, classify the event into one of the three IMCA categories, identify the initiating event as distinct from its consequences, and complete a draft station keeping event report containing: timeline, initiating event, consequences, response actions taken, and classification with one sentence of justification.
professional_standard: Handwritten timeline captures the event onset within 30 seconds of the system log time
First correct response action taken before turning to documentation — vessel first, paperwork second
Initiating event and consequences separated correctly in the report — the alarm you saw first is often not the initiating event
Classification defensible against the written definitions, stated in one sentence
Report complete enough that a DPO who was not present could reconstruct the event from it alone

fields.label: Time from onset to first correct response action (seconds)

debrief_questions: Walk through why you chose the classification you did — and what single change to the scenario would have pushed it into the category above or below?
What is the difference between the initiating event and the first alarm you noticed, and why do reports that confuse the two mislead the industry?
Why does the IMCA scheme publish events anonymously, and what reporting behaviours does that anonymity exist to protect against?
How does an initiating event differ from a root cause, and which one does your report identify?
On your vessel, who does a station keeping event report go to, and what should happen to it after that?

variants.title: Compound Event Report
variants.note_to_tdpo: Two degradations, close together. One timeline, one report, one classification for the combined event. Deciding whether it is one event or two is part of the task.

variants.title: Report a Clean Session
variants.note_to_tdpo: Nothing is injected, but something in any session is worth sharing — a reference wander, a load spike, a near-limit excursion. Find it, document it, and justify it as a DP observation. Learning to see reportable material in a normal watch is the point.

tasks.title: Emergency Procedure Touch Drill Circuit
tasks.setup: Vessel settled in DP at datum and holding throughout — the touch drill runs over a live station keeping picture, not a frozen screen. Select three emergency procedures from your vessel's DP operations manual (for example: loss of a position reference, loss of a thruster, initiation of the drive off response). For each, have the written procedure available but face down. A touch drill means physically touching or pointing to each control, page, or indicator in sequence — never actuating anything. The simulator state must be identical at the end to the start.
tasks.execute: Round one: for each of the three procedures in turn, execute the full response as a touch drill from memory — touch each control in order, say each step aloud, and time yourself. Then turn the written procedure over and mark every step you missed, added, or performed out of sequence. Round two: repeat all three drills. Record time and error count per drill per round. Confirm at the end that nothing was actuated and the DP picture is unchanged.
professional_standard: Every step physically located — touched or pointed to — not just named from the chair
Nothing actuated at any point; vessel position, heading and system state identical before and after
Round two error count lower than round one on every drill
Round two times faster than round one without steps being skipped to achieve it
Missed steps identified honestly against the written procedure, not rationalised away

fields.label: Round 1 errors per drill (missed/added/out of sequence, x3)
Steps most commonly missed across all drills

debrief_questions: Which steps did you miss in round one, and what do they have in common — are they the steps you understand least, or the ones that feel too obvious to rehearse?
Why does physically touching each control build a different kind of recall than reading the procedure or reciting it?
In a real emergency, which of your three procedures gives you the least time to think, and does your round two time for it reflect that?
What is the risk of touch drilling a procedure incorrectly and never checking against the written version — and what does that say about how this task should always be run?
Which procedure on your vessel would you touch drill next, and why that one?

variants.title: Cold Touch Drill

changes.trigger: Supervising DPO names one of the three procedures at an unannounced moment during a routine hold

variants.note_to_tdpo: No warm-up, no choosing the order. One procedure, called cold, timed. This is closer to how the real thing arrives.

variants.title: Cross-Station Touch Drill

changes.station: Perform the same three drills at the backup DP station

variants.note_to_tdpo: Same procedures, different desk. Notice which parts of your recall were tied to muscle memory of one console layout rather than to the procedure itself. Pairs naturally with er_001.
